program_note:
In Expanded Universe, my first book of Preludes and Fugues (2020-2021), I explored synthetic modes or scales that ranged anywhere from an octave and a half to six octaves in size.  Only one prelude and fugue—No.13 in C Lydian—used a pre-existing mode.  While the pitch-language was exploratory, however, it called for piano played with ordinary piano technique.
Parallel Universes, my second book of Preludes and Fugues (2021-2022) does the much the opposite.  Its approach to the piano is very different:  the instrument is prepared in advance, meaning that all manner of objects—from screws and blu-tack (poster putty) to chopsticks, sponges, paper, snare-drum snares and a beach towel—are positioned on the strings.  The alterations to the sound—the timbre—of the piano reminded me of several world music traditions, which in turn suggested modes or scales used in the piece:  about half of the scales or modes are drawn from musical traditions from around the world (including China, Indonesia, and Eastern European Klezmer).  Thus while the pitch-language is more conservative, the “sound language” is much more exploratory.
Parallel Universes is written for gradually-less-prepared piano:  if the entire set is played together, on the whole more preparations are removed than are added over the course of the set.  To facilitate performance of the entire set, the music is written for two pianos, each with different sets of preparations.  Ideally the set would be performed by two pianists, alternating on the two pianos:  while one plays the next prelude and fugue, the other makes the necessary alterations to the preparations (an assistant can help with those preparation alterations).  Since the “regular” piano sound gets gradually revealed, and since there would be two pianists performing, the set culminates in a two-piano duo for ordinary (unprepared) piano.

David S. Lefkowitz
16 September, 2022
Los Angeles, CA
